Two fixes, both to the socket, and the first of them is that the socket did not work at all against a real gateway. **90 of IBKR's 108 Trading endpoints, plus the socket**, as in `v0.4.0-preview.3`.

```sh
dotnet add package IbkrDotNet.Extensions.DependencyInjection --prerelease
```

## The read loop dropped every frame a Client Portal Gateway sent

`IbkrStreamingTransport`'s read loop dispatched a message only when it arrived as `WebSocketMessageType.Text`, with no `else`. The Client Portal Gateway sends **every** frame as binary carrying UTF-8 JSON — the session confirmation, the account and authentication-status messages, every heartbeat, every quote — so each one was received, reassembled, and then discarded at the top of the next iteration ([#69](https://github.com/jerbersoft/ibkrdotnet/issues/69)).

Nothing about that looked wrong. The transport reported `Connected`, `SubscribeAsync` succeeded, subscribe frames went out and were answered — and no subscription ever yielded a message, `LastHeartbeatAt` was never set, and `IsBrokerageSessionAuthenticated` was never learned. The symptom is indistinguishable from a socket that is simply quiet, which is what made it expensive to find.

A client connected to a gateway on 2026-09-17 counted six frames on the wire before the first heartbeat and not one of them text. In a separate 130-second window the gateway's own log recorded 299 `smd` frames sent to a subscribed client, while a heap dump of that client taken mid-window showed the subscription correctly registered, `DroppedMessages` at zero, its channel empty, and the read loop parked in `ReceiveAsync` — reading everything, routing nothing.

Text and binary are now dispatched the same, because the payload is UTF-8 JSON either way. `Close` had already broken out of the loop above and the enum has no fourth member, so the type check had no case left to make.

No test could express this: the scripted `WebSocket` the streaming tests drive reported `Text` whatever was queued, so every test exercised the one branch that worked. It now reports the type it was given and can queue a binary message, and the fix is pinned by a test that pushes one.

## An `ntf` message carries a list, and one payload of it is a prompt

`StreamingNotification` typed the topic's `args` as a single object — `id`, `title`, `text`, `url` — which is IBKR's published example. A paper gateway sends `args` as an **array**, and one of the two payloads recorded in it is not a notification at all but the limit-price constraint prompt: `orderId`, `reqId`, `messageId: "p12"`, three `options` and `prompt: true`, arriving unsolicited rather than as the answer to a submission ([#68](https://github.com/jerbersoft/ibkrdotnet/issues/68)).

Read through the old model the first frame failed outright, and the second would have come back as a notification holding nothing but its text — losing the order it names, the identifier the answer is sent back with, and the three answers on offer.

`StreamingNotification.Args` is now a list, read so that IBKR's documented bare object still deserializes, and each element is one of two shapes: a `StreamingNotificationArgs.Notice`, carrying `Id`, `Title` and `Url`, or a `StreamingNotificationArgs.Prompt`, carrying the order by IBKR's own numeric identifier along with `RequestId`, `MessageId`, `Options`, `Type` and `Dismissable`. `Text` sits on the base, because both shapes have one.

They are two types rather than one record with everything optional so that answering a prompt does not begin with working out whether the payload was one. `Prompt.OrderId` and `RequestId` are exactly what `IOrdersClient.DismissServerPromptAsync` takes, and `MessageId` is the category `SuppressMessagesAsync` silences — the endpoints were already there, with no way to learn that one of these had arrived. IBKR marks neither shape with a type tag, so a payload is told by the fields it carries; anything carrying `orderId`, `messageId` or `prompt` is read as a prompt, because dropping a question is worse than reading a notice that gained a field.

## What this breaks

`StreamingNotificationArgs` is now abstract and `StreamingNotification.Args` is a list, so `notification.Args?.Title` becomes a pattern match over `notification.Args`. That is the whole of the transcript's change, and nothing else in the library read the type.

Worth saying plainly: against a real gateway nobody can have been reading an `ntf` message successfully, because of the other fix in this release. The break is real for a consumer testing against a scripted socket, and theoretical for one connected to a gateway.

## Nothing else changed

563 tests, five of them new. Both recorded `ntf` frames ship as `notifications.live.json`, beside IBKR's published example. The scripted `WebSocket` gained the ability to queue a binary message and to report the type it was queued with, which is what makes the transport fix testable at all.

## Why this is still a prerelease

For the reason `v0.4.0-preview.1` gave — the public API is still settling — and this release argues the rest of the case by itself. A defect that made streaming deliver nothing survived 558 tests and three previews, because every one of those tests drove a fake that could not send what a gateway sends. That is the shape of thing only a live run catches, and [#60](https://github.com/jerbersoft/ibkrdotnet/issues/60) is still open: the socket has now been driven against a gateway far enough to find this, but the sweep and the `.live.json` capture it tracks are not done.

## Publishing

Pushed by [Trusted Publishing](https://learn.microsoft.com/nuget/nuget-org/trusted-publishing) over OIDC, as the previous four versions were; both packages are also attached to this release.
